Mława Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Mława, Poland

Demolished. Mława, granted Chełmno city rights in 1429, saw early Jewish settlement tied to Russian trade, amid recurring conflicts including mid-16th-century ritual-murder accusations; only 5 of 429 houses were Jewish-owned by 1564. A 1776 Catholic-led expulsion order interrupted settlement until 1790; by 1857, Jews made up 50% (1,650) of the town, reaching 45% (7,017) by 1910 after an 1877 railway boosted trade. Mława saw major September 1939 fighting, with Jews participating in its defense; incorporated into the Reich that October, about 3,000 Jews were deported to Działdowo and 4,000 more to distant ghettos by early 1940, replaced by Jews relocated from ten nearby towns into a new December 1940 ghetto. By late 1942, 6,000-7,000 were deported to Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau; only 20 survivors returned after the war, with the last, Józef Poznański, dying in 1956. This cemetery, confirmed active by 1775 and likely operating for at least 50 years before that, closed in the second half of the 19th century when adjacent military facilities expanded; Germans used its stones in 1941 to build a military complex ('Second Berlin') near Nosarzewo, where matzevot fragments remain visible embedded in two standing columns.
